slot.brief: Use Euler-type substitution t = x + √(x² + k) to rationalise and integrate an expression with √(x² + k).

stem: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_0^{1/2} \dfrac{dx}{(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 2})^3}$ is equal to

verdicts.working: Substitute t = x+√(x²+2) ⇒ x=(t²−2)/(2t), dx=(t²+2)/(2t²)dt. Integral becomes ∫(t²+2)/(2t⁵)dt = −(1/4)(t⁻²+t⁻⁴). Limits: x=0→t=√2; x=1/2→t=2. Value = −(1/4)[(1/4+1/16)−(1/2+1/4)] = 7/64 ≈ 0.109375, confirmed by Simpson numerical integration.

working:
We use the Euler substitution of the first kind:
$$t = x + \sqrt{x^2 + 2}$$
Then:
$$t - x = \sqrt{x^2 + 2} \implies (t - x)^2 = x^2 + 2 \implies t^2 - 2tx = 2 \implies x = \dfrac{t^2 - 2}{2t} = \dfrac{t}{2} - \dfrac{1}{t}$$
Differentiating with respect to $t$:
$$dx = \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{t^2}\right) dt = \dfrac{t^2 + 2}{2t^2}\,dt$$
Now find the new limits of integration:
- At $x = 0$: $t = 0 + \sqrt{0 + 2} = \sqrt{2}$
- At $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$: $t = \dfrac{1}{2} + \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4} + 2} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2} = 2$

Substitute into the integral:
$$I = \int_{\sqrt{2}}^2 \dfrac{1}{t^3} \cdot \dfrac{t^2 + 2}{2t^2}\,dt = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\sqrt{2}}^2 \left(t^{-3} + 2t^{-5}\right) dt$$
Integrating term by term:
$$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{2t^2} - \dfrac{2}{4t^4} \right]_{\sqrt{2}}^2 = -\dfrac{1}{4} \left[ \dfrac{1}{t^2} + \dfrac{1}{t^4} \right]_{\sqrt{2}}^2$$
Evaluating at the upper limit $t = 2$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2^2} + \dfrac{1}{2^4} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{5}{16}$$
Evaluating at the lower limit $t = \sqrt{2}$:
$$\dfrac{1}{(\sqrt{2})^2} + \dfrac{1}{(\sqrt{2})^4} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{12}{16}$$
Thus:
$$I = -\dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{5}{16} - \dfrac{12}{16}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{4} \left(-\dfrac{7}{16}\right) = \dfrac{7}{64}$$

Independent check: Substitute t = x+√(x²+2) ⇒ x=(t²−2)/(2t), dx=(t²+2)/(2t²)dt. Integral becomes ∫(t²+2)/(2t⁵)dt = −(1/4)(t⁻²+t⁻⁴). Limits: x=0→t=√2; x=1/2→t=2. Value = −(1/4)[(1/4+1/16)−(1/2+1/4)] = 7/64 ≈ 0.109375, confirmed by Simpson numerical integration.

draft.stem: The value of the integral $\displaystyle\int_0^{1/2} \dfrac{dx}{(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 2})^3}$ is equal to
draft.working:
We use the Euler substitution of the first kind:
$$t = x + \sqrt{x^2 + 2}$$
Then:
$$t - x = \sqrt{x^2 + 2} \implies (t - x)^2 = x^2 + 2 \implies t^2 - 2tx = 2 \implies x = \dfrac{t^2 - 2}{2t} = \dfrac{t}{2} - \dfrac{1}{t}$$
Differentiating with respect to $t$:
$$dx = \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{t^2}\right) dt = \dfrac{t^2 + 2}{2t^2}\,dt$$
Now find the new limits of integration:
- At $x = 0$: $t = 0 + \sqrt{0 + 2} = \sqrt{2}$
- At $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$: $t = \dfrac{1}{2} + \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4} + 2} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2} = 2$

Substitute into the integral:
$$I = \int_{\sqrt{2}}^2 \dfrac{1}{t^3} \cdot \dfrac{t^2 + 2}{2t^2}\,dt = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\sqrt{2}}^2 \left(t^{-3} + 2t^{-5}\right) dt$$
Integrating term by term:
$$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{2t^2} - \dfrac{2}{4t^4} \right]_{\sqrt{2}}^2 = -\dfrac{1}{4} \left[ \dfrac{1}{t^2} + \dfrac{1}{t^4} \right]_{\sqrt{2}}^2$$
Evaluating at the upper limit $t = 2$:
$$\dfrac{1}{2^2} + \dfrac{1}{2^4} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{5}{16}$$
Evaluating at the lower limit $t = \sqrt{2}$:
$$\dfrac{1}{(\sqrt{2})^2} + \dfrac{1}{(\sqrt{2})^4} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{12}{16}$$
Thus:
$$I = -\dfrac{1}{4} \left(\dfrac{5}{16} - \dfrac{12}{16}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{4} \left(-\dfrac{7}{16}\right) = \dfrac{7}{64}$$
draft.distractor_notes:
Option A corresponds to evaluating only at the upper limit $t = 2$ and mistakenly assuming the lower limit evaluates to zero.
Option C corresponds to forgetting the factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in the differential $dx = \dfrac{t^2+2}{2t^2}\,dt$, yielding $2 \times \dfrac{7}{64} = \dfrac{7}{32}$.
Option D corresponds to forgetting the division by the exponents when integrating $t^{-3}$ and $t^{-5}$, resulting in an answer larger by a factor of $4$.
